definition: New and unlike anything seen or done before.
example: The engineers found a novel way to cool the building using collected rainwater.
nuance: Novel stresses originality, not recency: a novel idea differs from earlier ones, while a new car may match last year's model.
prompt: A science fair judge is reviewing student projects.
options: The judge praised the student's novel method of measuring plant growth with a phone camera.
The judge called the project novel because it copied last year's winner step by step.
The judge called the report novel because it ran to three hundred pages, divided into chapters.
The judge called the volcano model novel simply because its glue was still wet.
reasons: An inventive approach no one had tried before is exactly what the word describes.
Copying an earlier project is the opposite of being original.
This confuses the adjective with the book sense; length and chapters don't make an idea original.
Being freshly made is not the same as being unlike anything before.

practice.prompt: A chef is planning the menu for her restaurant's opening night.
options: The salad was novel because its lettuce had been picked only an hour before dinner.
The chef called the portions novel because each plate now cost twice as much as before.
The chef's novel pairing of roasted pears with miso surprised even experienced diners.
The chef planned a novel menu made up entirely of dishes every diner in town already knew by heart.
reasons: Fresh ingredients are recent, but that does not make the dish original.
A higher price says nothing about whether something is new in kind.
An unexpected combination that diners had never tasted shows true originality.
Dishes everyone already knows are familiar, which reverses the meaning.
